title: How do restaurants and fast-food chains make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Restaurant economics for case interviews: covers, average spend, food and labour costs, franchising and delivery apps, with a worked unit-economics example.
hook: Restaurant cases are popular because everyone understands the product. Underneath, they test unit economics: what one restaurant earns, what it costs to run, and how chains grow through franchising.
body:
The basic equation

Revenue = covers (customers served) × average spend. The biggest costs are usually food and labour, followed by rent.

A worked example: one restaurant's profit

A fast-casual restaurant serves 400 customers a day at £10 each, 360 days a year: £1.44M revenue. If food is 30% (£432k), labour 30% (£432k), rent and other costs 25% (£360k), it keeps 15%, about £216k a year. If it cost £600k to open, payback is under three years.

Franchising

Many chains let franchisees own and run restaurants, taking a royalty on sales. The chain earns less per restaurant but grows faster with less money and risk (see business models).

Delivery apps

Apps bring orders but charge high commissions, which can turn a profitable order into a loss. The profitability guide works through exactly this problem.

Typical restaurant case questions

  • Why are profits falling despite stable sales?
  • Should we expand through franchising?
  • Should we launch a delivery-only kitchen?

Calculate restaurant profit before choosing a growth lever

A fast-casual restaurant serves 250 customers per day with an average spend of £12 and opens 300 days a year. Sales are 250 × £12 × 300 = £900,000. Suppose ingredients and packaging consume 32% of sales, staff 28%, rent 12% and other operating expenses 18%. Total operating costs are 90% of revenue, leaving approximately £90,000 operating profit, a 10% margin on these made-up assumptions.

Now the restaurant starts using a delivery platform. The platform generates £120,000 of annual orders, but half replace orders customers previously placed directly. Incremental revenue is therefore only £60,000 before any menu-price differences. If the platform charges 25% commission on all £120,000, commissions total £30,000. The owner must still pay for ingredients, packaging and delivery-specific labour. Gross delivery sales are not the same as incremental profit.

In a chain-expansion case, model one location first: demand, orders per day, average ticket, gross margin, rent, labour and required investment. Then ask if the model holds at the next site. A busy flagship near an office district may not predict sales in a suburban area with different lunch traffic.

For a restaurant with declining profits, split on-premise, takeaway and delivery channels. Check whether menu prices, ingredient costs, portion sizes, staffing and channel mix changed. The first insight may be that sales grew while profit fell because each extra order went through a more expensive channel.
outro: Next in this topic: How do online retailers make money, and what matters in an e-commerce case?
